meta.title: Where is all the new, good software?
meta.author: gerikson

comments.author: elliotmorris
comments.text:
Some of these may be true in the fullness of time.

However, I suspect the question is wrong. "Where is all the good new software?" belies an assumption that the point of the software economy is to produce utility for the consumer. AI may justify itself via a reduction in the labour expense of existing entrenched companies, where the utility of what they produce is almost a secondary concern and can even be allowed to fall so long as their entrenchment can bear it.

This would mean that AI coding could be effective, but still lead to overall worse software and generally poor outcomes.

If true, this is a societal conflict of interest that needs to be resolved, probably by means other than market forces.

comments.author: sethetter
comments.text:
Whether the quality of the software (by whatever measures that entails) matters most in the success of a given product has arguably always depended on the market. Look at MS products, for example.

However, for some customers quality matters more and they might choose a different product. I believe that's separate from whether AI is able to or intended to improve quality or just quantity.

AI tools let us focus more on features (fast and loose) or quality (more rigorous tests, time spent experimenting and refining, etc). All comes down to what the team / business wielding it chooses to focus their tokens efforts into.

Also: I think we're still, as an industry, figuring out how to best utilize AI for either of the above outcomes, so even if a company is trying to use AI to improve quality, they just may not have quite cracked that nut yet.

Software teams are capturing a lot of the speedup in the form of more leisure or quasi-leisure time. (To greatly simplify: software teams are offering 2x speedups to their companies. They're then using tools that allow them to work 10x as efficiently, and taking nice long coffee breaks.)


There's an important flip side to this, which is the actual mental model overhead.

Unless you're doing slop, you'll need to think about your code. That 2-3x speedup might actually be the limit of your cognition, at least in matters of direct human-on-keyboard work for your employer. Those coffee breaks are necessary, and sometimes downright essential.

For the rest of the post - pretty much (a bit of) all of the above. I've conjectured that we'll have far more smaller software and abandon SaaS that isn't exceptional, and it seems to be happening. I've seen a fair few overblown SaaS companies needing to scale down.

I'm not overly motivated to publish them widely or spend marketing/sales budget, but it was fun and brings me utility every day. Can't complain about the impact of LLM software on myself. Services I use daily, though, don't seem as improved as I'd enjoy.

comments.author: greysonp
comments.text:
I always thought the claim of "if LLM's are so great, where is all the new software?" to be a little funny. Pre-LLMs, we would look at a company's employee growth, like Twitter having 5k employees, and people would be like "how is it that this little webapp has so many people working on it, but no new features?" And the common refrain would be "It's scale! So much of the software written at twitter isn't to add a new feature, but to maintain infra, support moderation, etc".

Now we have a similar situation where companies have "grown" (in the sense that overall throughput has been non-trivially increased), and people still ask the same question, and I feel like the answer is still the same -- code is disproportionally allocated towards tooling, infra, etc, just like it always has been. Google Docs has barely changed in 10 years and it'll continue to barely change.

There has been a ton of cool new software that has come from LLMs. One category of work is game recomps and decomps, where people rebuild games (like the well-known Pokemon gen1recomp) to be self-sustaining executables with modding support. These efforts are almost entirely LLM-driven and have been very fun.

Personally I'm less interested in using LLMs to accelerate development of new features, and more interested them in using them to build a feature in the same amount of time, but with increased robustness and reliability.

comments.author: elliotmorris
comments.text:
The implied question behind "where is all the new software?" is often "how does this new technology justify its costs?" Growing the market with new, better software is the most obvious route to this in many peoples minds, but equally they could be asking "where is all the economically measurable productivity?"

That might all be in internal tooling, infra, etc, but it is not acceptable for this technology to barely change anything from an externally observable economic perspective, it has to be radically impactful in measurable ways for all this AI debt to be justified.

comments.author: yshui
comments.text:
AI doesn't work well with humans, and I believe that's an early manifestation of a misaligned AI.

AI is very good at churn out a large amount of code that achieves some predefined goal. This is very evident by looking at the number of game porting/decompilation projects, and software reverse engineering projects that sprung up overnight like mushrooms. The problem is the code they write is horrendous, and this sentiment is echoed by mathematicians who have read the math proofs generated by AI as well[1].

Direct consequence of this is that it's basically impossible to integrate AI into a traditional software engineering process. The amount of code AI churns out is huge, the quality of the code in terms of human readability and maintainability is so terrible, code review just cannot catch up. [2]

And fundamentally this is because AI just does not understand what a human wants. In other word, this is an AI alignment problem.

[1]: Tristan Buckmaster, talking about his work on the Euler Equation: I can say the first LLM generated proof Levent sent me was the most horrendous I have ever read; we verified it on Lean on August 22nd. Since this point, we have been working around the clock to understand this proof and turn it into something readable.

[2]: https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/10/ai-coding-agents-generate-more-code-but-not-more-software/ A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them.

We are in fact seeing software improvement, in the form of fewer bugs and better performance.

Often when raising that something is broken, the answer is usually "Claude can fix it" (work around). Which...if we build a culture of workarounds for workarounds then finding and fixing the root of problems becomes socially harder and harder. LLMs are good at finding bugs, they're not always good at gauging the relative importance of which are trivial and which are important.

You can write high rigor software aided by LLMs, but it is not the norm or the default for most users.

comments.text:
By the way, where the edge of meta lies? Does making dictation more convenient count, if I use a public-weights NN in the middle of the pipeline?

I want dictation, and it is much easier to set up fragment-by-fragment recognition than true streaming. All software I know for cutting a recording into fragments on silence uses absolute total levels. With any kind of background noise it is … meh.

I was clearly not getting around to learning ALSA interface Right Now™, so I asked a local LLM to capture, build a spectrum histogram via FFT, and compare to the background noise profile bucket-by-bucket. So much easier to set thresholds than total volume dB thresholds, it's not even funny.

It does do what I wanted it to do, it is truly vipe-coded slop, I skimmed it and slopped (or sometimes did by hand) a few fixes where I thought it's too much even for slop, some places it industriously made better than I would lazily do. But it is all to better feed data to Whisper. Is it ML-meta?

The idea is trivial, the implementation is small-ish, but nobody that I can easily find published code for it, and I am lazy, so here we are. I might put it into some publically reachable landfill, but maybe I should properly check first that it does not do anything weird with unrelated files. For own use, I sandbox it, so I wouldn't notice.

comments.author: pm
comments.text:
The problem with posts like this is they are just claims with no evidence.

I don't like to take sides on what is essentially reality. AI exists and people use it. For them, it is useful. That's not really a debate.
If the benefits outweigh the negatives on the grand scheme of things, becomes a philosophical question.

On the specific case of software being produced here and now, it is worth noticing that the problems people attribute to AI, were already manifesting themselves in industrial scale before the advent of AI coding tools.

Reinventing the wheel everywhere, software riddled with bugs every other click, UIs and workflows driven by trends and how slick they look rather than how effective they are at a specific task. Corporate Godzilla sized  distributed systems that often could be called down to a $100 server. Gigabyte size binaries that pack the same functionality than a 200kB program written in the 1990s.

On the face of all this, we blame AI... I don't buy it.

comments.author: atmosx
comments.text:
The tl;dr : There is no MAP-E CE implementation in OpenBSD.

The project: https://github.com/atmosx/openbsd-mape-ce/tree/main

Long version

My ISP switched to MAP-E CE for FTTH in mid-2024. I was already running an OpenBSD router behind double NAT. Then things happened, and I suddenly found myself with a testing environment, so I figured I'd give it a shot.

MAP-E CE is a relatively new technology used by ISPs, with several advantages over alternatives like CGNAT. As far as I know, it's properly supported only by Linux/OpenWrt. FreeBSD has partial support, while other systems have none.

MAP-E CE uses IPv4-over-IPv6 encapsulation, and the system needs to know which range of shared public IPv4 ports the ISP has assigned to the customer, the algorithm to do the calculation and obviously needs to perform encapsulation and decapsulation. This means patching PF to handle the required port mapping (outgoing IPv4 connections must use ports from the assigned range), as well as adding Softwire46 support to dhcp6leased to obtain the necessary configuration via DHCPv6.

This project has cost me both money (mostly credits for frontier AI models) and, more importantly, time. Lots of time spent testing, debugging, retrying, and polishing. Still, I'm happy with the results so far, and I'm already preparing a second installation. Lets say that it wasn't easy or straight forward.

It's been fun and a great learning experience, although, tbh, I'd much rather have all of this in the base system, handle upgrades with sysmerge, and call it a day. :-)

comments.author: nathell
comments.text:
I've been vibecoding a piece of software for my own use, and it's... good and not good at the same time.

It works pretty well. It solves a real need. It's novel – no existing solutions solve my exact problem, or else I would have opted to use those. It's been fast to develop and ~ instant to add new features as I discover myself needing them. The design is sound. So it's all good in those senses.

It's not good in that ... it's slop. It's ~200 KB of very LLM-y code that's hard to follow at times. It feels overengineered – I think the implementation can be simplified to the benefit of both the user and code quality.

I'll be open-sourcing it anyway shortly, and my plan is to then take my time to study the code carefully and make it closer to what I would have written manually. For now, my emotions about it are a quantum superposition of elation and grudge. Part of the elation is due to the fact that I can, and will, dogfood it to study itself!

What we need is a new paradigm: generic, data-driven platforms where the application is data, run by one well-tested engine.

code built on stable foundation needs drastically less maintenance


Agreed, and that is the case for the paradigm. In LinkedDataHub, which I build, so I am not neutral, the foundation is RDF, SPARQL and XSLT, whose current versions date from 2013 to 2017. The application-specific part is data. A document does not need rebuilding when the engine is updated.


Sounds like something where inner platform effect will be unbeatable


Only if the platform is invented in-house. Here the application is written in the web's own standards, and the engine is generic the way a browser is generic. The effect shows up when the declarations drift into an ad hoc DSL, and these do not.

What's innacurate? People want LLM provenance to be labeled. You may quibble with the term (e.g. "vibecoding") chosen by the community, but it's the term the community settled on for describing the provenance, and it really boils down to identifying LLM provenance at the end of the day.


Attempts at accuracy are met with violence


Please show me an example of violence directed toward someone who wants accuracy in the description of software provenance! I've not witnessed that.

comments.author: gerikson
comments.text:
There is no "ai-generated" tag.


If you don't, a moderator will rush to do it.


Most tag changes to "vibecoding" are made by users: https://lobste.rs/moderations?moderator=%28All%29&what%5Bstories%5D=stories

comments.author: vrypan
comments.text:
Fair, but "vibecoding" is even more degrading.

I get it that each forum and each community have the right to set their rules, but then no one will share what they worked on for months there, if they have to slap some insulting label to it.

It's like asking every indie project to be tagged "amateur hour", and then wonder "where are the good indie projects".

comments.author: gnyeki
comments.text: I treat vibecoding as a neutral tag and decide whether to engage with the post based on the content. The tag has an unfortunate name (llm-usage would be better) but that doesn’t force me to interpret it either negatively or positively. I think folks who are active on here have figured that out by now.
